questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A button labelled with a noun
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a control's label tells the reader what will happen
questions.stem: A confirmation dialog offers two buttons, labelled Confirm and Cancellation. What has the label of the first button left the reader without?

options.text: A sense of what confirming will do, since the label names the act and not its object
A way to close the dialog, since the second button provides one
options.misconception: misses that a second button is present, and the fault is in the first label

options.text: Any way to tell the two buttons apart, since one is Confirm and one is not
options.misconception: supposes a labelling failure where the two labels are plainly distinct

options.text: An instruction to read the rest of the dialog first, which no dialog supplies
options.misconception: demands a courtesy a dialog has no room for, when the label is the failing part

questions.explanation: A control label is read in a fraction of a second, in parallel with everything else on the screen, and it has to survive that. Confirm is an instruction with no object: it tells the reader that pressing the button confirms something and nothing about what. A reader who is closing a bank transfer needs to know whether the money will move, whether a contract will be signed, whether a message will be delivered to forty people, and Confirm gives them none of that. The same shortcoming has a second-order effect, because a dialog whose buttons both read as verbs of the same kind makes the two options harder to compare, and a reader who cannot compare the buttons is more likely to take the default. Neither of the other two claims about the second button is right, since it does close the dialog, and a dialog is not obliged to instruct the reader to read it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader learns from the label that they could not see from the rest of the screen.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A destructive action with a neutral label
questions.learningObjective: judge the label of a control that cannot be undone

stimulus.body: DIALOG TITLE: Remove item. BODY TEXT: This will remove the selected rows from the view. This cannot be undone. BUTTONS: OK | Cancel. The dialog is the last of four steps and the first three have already been completed.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A dialog reads: 'DIALOG TITLE: Remove item. BODY TEXT: This will remove the selected rows from the view. This cannot be undone. BUTTONS: OK | Cancel. The dialog is the last of four steps and the first three have already been completed.' What has the labelling failed to do?

options.text: Warn the reader at all, since the body text already says the action cannot be undone
options.misconception: misses that the warning is in the body, where a reader comparing buttons does not see it

options.text: Put the consequence on the button, so the choice is legible from the control itself
Name what is being removed, since the title says only that an item is involved
options.misconception: misses that the body names the rows, and the fault is on the button not the title

options.text: Give the two buttons different lengths, so they are easier to tell apart at a glance
options.misconception: asks for a visual distinction, where the failing element is the word OK rather than the size

questions.explanation: The dialog has done the hard part and spent its effort in the wrong place. The body says what will happen, that selected rows will be removed from the view, and that it cannot be undone, which is the information a reader needs. Both facts are then placed where a reader is least likely to look, because a reader who has reached a dialog with two buttons is comparing the buttons, and OK says nothing at all: not what it removes, not that it is final, not that it is the dangerous one. The label is what survives when the body is skimmed, and OK is the shortest possible way of ensuring nothing survives. Note also that remove from the view is a softer claim than delete, and the body cannot make up for a button that offers the reader no way to tell which of the two they are choosing.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words a reader is looking at when they choose.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: An error message with no next step
questions.learningObjective: judge what an error message has to hand the reader

stimulus.body: ERROR: 4001. The request could not be completed. Try again later. If the problem continues, contact support. The message is the whole of the page and the only control on it is a Close button.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A message reads: 'ERROR: 4001. The request could not be completed. Try again later. If the problem continues, contact support. The message is the whole of the page and the only control on it is a Close button.' What has the message failed to give the reader?

options.text: A cause, which every error message is obliged to name in full
options.misconception: demands a cause the system may not be able to give, and the fault is the absence of any action

options.text: A code, which the message supplies at the start and a reader can quote
options.misconception: misses the code that is already printed in the first line of the message

options.text: A step that would fix it, since a reader is left with the same options they had before
An apology, since a message that does not apologise is discourteous to a reader
options.misconception: supplies a tone requirement, when a message is measured by what it lets a reader do

questions.explanation: Try later and contact support are the two halves of an instruction to do something a reader cannot usefully do. Try again later is plausible when the fault is a server that is busy and useless when the request will fail identically every time, and the message gives a reader nothing to distinguish the two cases. Contact support is plausible when the fault is on the reader's side and useless when it is not, and a reader who follows it hands a stranger an error code and nothing else to go on. What a message of this kind owes the reader is one thing they can do that they could not do before, whether that is a different value, a different route, or a named person to write to. The other three answers each ask for something the message either supplies, cannot supply, or need not supply.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do after reading this that they could not do before.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: An error message that blames the reader
questions.learningObjective: judge an error message written to assign fault

stimulus.body: ERROR: You entered the date incorrectly. The date must be in the format DD/MM/YYYY. Check your entry and try again. The field is the fifth of eight on a form, it is empty, and the reader reached it for the first time half a minute ago.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A message reads: 'ERROR: You entered the date incorrectly. The date must be in the format DD/MM/YYYY. Check your entry and try again. The field is the fifth of eight on a form, it is empty, and the reader reached it for the first time half a minute ago.' What is the problem with the first line?

options.text: It repeats the word incorrectly, so the message says the same thing twice
options.misconception: counts a repetition, when the fault is the certainty of a claim about the reader

options.text: It mentions the format before giving a date, so the instruction arrives out of order
options.misconception: invents an ordering problem, when the format is what lets a reader fix the entry

options.text: It uses the pronoun you, which a message about a system should avoid
options.misconception: objects to a pronoun, where every line of the message uses it and the fault lies elsewhere

options.text: It asserts what the reader did when the field may never have been filled in at all

questions.explanation: You entered the date incorrectly is a claim about the past, and the system's most common situation does not support it. A field that has been left empty has not been entered incorrectly; a field the reader has not yet reached has not been entered at all; a value the system has lost in transit has not been entered by anybody. So the message asserts a completed act by a particular agent in a case where the commonest cause is that no act took place, and it does so in a way that makes a first-time reader feel they have already failed once. Nothing about the rest of the message is wrong: the format is the instruction a reader needs, and check your entry and try again is a reasonable next step once the field has something in it. The defect is the certainty of the first clause.
questions.hint: Ask what the system knows at the moment it shows this message.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A hint that contradicts its own field
questions.learningObjective: judge a field whose hint and validation cannot both be met

stimulus.body: FIELD LABEL: Date of birth. FIELD HINT: Enter as DD/MM/YYYY, for example 14/03/1998. VALIDATION MESSAGE: Dates may not be entered in the future. VALIDATION MESSAGE: Enter the date as four digits, for example 1998-03-14.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A form carries: 'FIELD LABEL: Date of birth. FIELD HINT: Enter as DD/MM/YYYY, for example 14/03/1998. VALIDATION MESSAGE: Dates may not be entered in the future. VALIDATION MESSAGE: Enter the date as four digits, for example 1998-03-14.' What is wrong with this?

options.text: The two instructions for the same field ask for formats that cannot both be the accepted one
The hint is shown after the label, when it ought to be shown before the reader types
options.misconception: invents a placement rule, when the contradiction is between the two instructions themselves

options.text: The example date 1998 is old, so it makes the field look out of date to a reader
options.misconception: objects to an example's year, which is chosen to be unambiguous rather than current

options.text: The second validation message duplicates the hint, so the form says the same thing twice
options.misconception: misses that a validation message and a hint are shown at different moments and may differ

questions.explanation: Two instructions for one field, and they do not agree. The hint asks for DD/MM/YYYY and gives an example in that form; the validation message asks for four digits and gives an example in ISO order, 1998-03-14. A reader cannot satisfy both, and the two are not even the same kind of thing: a four-digit year is not a format, it is a component, and the message that contains it also supplies a complete date in a different order. Whichever of the two the form actually accepts, the other is wrong on the page, and a reader who followed the first instruction and was rejected has been actively misled rather than merely left uninformed. The other three answers each raise a point about placement, about an example's date, or about repetition, and none of them survives the fact that the two instructions are mutually exclusive.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who follows the hint will be told when they submit.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Grey field text doing a label's work
questions.learningObjective: judge a field whose label is only a placeholder

stimulus.body: FIELD: an empty box with the grey text Enter your email address inside it. No other text appears above or beside the box. On focus the grey text disappears. The form has no other label for this box.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A form has: 'FIELD: an empty box with the grey text Enter your email address inside it. No other text appears above or beside the box. On focus the grey text disappears. The form has no other label for this box.' What has the form lost?

options.text: A default value, so a reader must type even where a sensible value could be supplied
options.misconception: asks for a convenience, when the form's failure is that its instruction disappears when needed

options.text: A label that stays on screen, so a reader who has typed has nothing to check the value against
An example, so a reader does not know what an address should look like
options.misconception: supplies a missing example, which is not the same as losing the label itself

options.text: A hint about the format, which the box does not supply and a reader will ask for
options.misconception: fixes on an absent hint while the label that is present is the one that vanishes

questions.explanation: The instruction and the label have been merged into one piece of text, and the merge fails at the moment it is needed. A label is a persistent name for a field: it is there before a reader types, it is there while they type, and it is there afterwards so that a value of fred@ has something to be checked against. Grey text inside a box disappears the instant the field is touched, which is precisely the moment a reader is most likely to have mistyped, and a form that supplies no other label therefore leaves a reader with an unreviewable value. There are cases where in-field text is enough, and they are forms with one field and no possibility of error. This is a form that asks for an email address, which is the single most mistyped field there is, and it has chosen the text that vanishes over the text that stays.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can see while they are typing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A required marker explained nowhere
questions.learningObjective: judge a form that marks a field without saying what the mark means
questions.stem: A form marks one field with an asterisk and gives no key anywhere on the page. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: An asterisk is a poor choice of mark, since it is also used to denote a footnote
options.misconception: objects to the character, when the fault is that no key explains it

options.text: A form should mark every field as required rather than marking only some
options.misconception: supposes a rule about marking, which no form is obliged to follow

options.text: A reader who has not met the convention before has no way to learn what the mark requires
A reader who fills the marked field wrongly will be told, so the mark is not needed
options.misconception: denies the mark a purpose, when the mark tells a reader before submitting rather than after

questions.explanation: A required marker works by borrowing a convention, and the convention is not universal. A reader who has filled in many forms will know what an asterisk means and a reader who has not will not, and the second reader is left to discover the requirement by submitting the form and being refused, which turns a sign into a test. The reason the mark is worth having at all is that it lets a reader see the whole shape of the form before starting, so a page of asterisks tells them in one glance what the submission will require. That benefit depends on the mark being explained once, either in a key beside the form or in the text of the button that submits it. The other three answers each object to the wrong thing: the character is serviceable, there is no rule about which fields are marked, and being told after submitting is precisely what the mark exists to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who has never seen the mark is being asked to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A password rule with no measurable threshold
questions.learningObjective: judge a requirement a reader cannot satisfy on purpose
questions.stem: A form requires that a password be strong and memorable. What is the strongest objection to the requirement as written?

options.text: The two requirements pull against each other, so no password can satisfy both
options.misconception: supplies a tension, which the two requirements do not create

options.text: A password is never memorable, so the second half of the rule is impossible
options.misconception: asserts an impossibility, when a reader can certainly remember a password they chose

options.text: Strength is a matter of opinion, so the form cannot enforce what it asks for
options.misconception: suggests opinion is the obstacle, when the obstacle is that neither word has a test

options.text: Neither term is measurable, so a reader cannot tell whether an entry complies

questions.explanation: A requirement is only useful to a reader if it can be satisfied deliberately. Strong and memorable are both judgements that a reader can form and a machine cannot apply, so a form that requires them has asked for something it has no way to check and a reader has no way to confirm. The two words also fail in different directions, which is worth noticing: memorable is a property of a password's owner and strong a property of the password, so a requirement that conjoins them describes a target rather than a test. What a form can state is a composition, at least this many characters and at least one of these kinds, and a reader can then satisfy it and know that they have. The other three answers each raise a difficulty that is not the difficulty here: the two halves do not conflict, a chosen password can certainly be remembered, and a judgement is not what stops a machine applying the rule.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could tell, before submitting, that they had met the rule.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A password rule stated in one sentence
questions.learningObjective: judge a single-sentence description of a multi-part rule

stimulus.body: HELP TEXT: Passwords must be at least twelve characters and must include a number, a capital letter and a symbol. The three of these are cumulative, so an entry missing any one of them is refused.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A form's help text reads: 'Passwords must be at least twelve characters and must include a number, a capital letter and a symbol. The three of these are cumulative, so an entry missing any one of them is refused.' What has the help text left a reader to work out?

options.text: Whether a password that meets all three is accepted, since nothing says the rules interact
Whether the twelve characters count the symbol, which the text does not say either way
options.misconception: raises a genuine gap, which is not the gap the second sentence fails to close

options.text: Which symbols are allowed, since the text says only that a symbol is required
options.misconception: asks for a list that a form can reasonably define elsewhere

options.text: Whether the rule applies to old passwords too, which the text does not mention
options.misconception: invents a scope question the sentence does not raise

questions.explanation: Two sentences are spent on a requirement that could have taken one, and the second sentence is spent on a question the reader did not ask. The first sentence gives the whole rule: twelve characters, a number, a capital letter and a symbol. What it does not say, and a reader coming to a new rule genuinely cannot guess, is how the parts stand to each other: whether any one of them can be traded for extra length, or whether all three are compulsory together. That is a real question and the first sentence leaves it open. The second sentence answers a different question, the one about whether missing any part is fatal, which a reader would probably have assumed, at the cost of a sentence that should have settled the live question. Nothing here is wrong, which is the difficulty: the reader is left with a rule they can follow and a rule they cannot predict.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would try first if length and composition were in tension.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A page title written for a list of results
questions.learningObjective: judge a title written for a machine rather than for a reader

stimulus.body: PAGE TITLE: Results 1-20 of 342 | Household waste collection calendar | Council services. PAGE HEADING: Search results. The list shows twenty records, each with a reference number, a date and a status word, and no explanation of what the status words mean.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A page carries: 'PAGE TITLE: Results 1-20 of 342 | Household waste collection calendar | Council services. PAGE HEADING: Search results. The list shows twenty records, each with a reference number, a date and a status word, and no explanation of what the status words mean.' What has been written for the wrong reader?

options.text: The heading, since Search results tells a reader nothing about what was searched for
options.misconception: fixes on the heading, when the title is the line written in the wrong register

options.text: The title, which is assembled for a list of results and reads as a row of fragments
The status words, since an unexplained word on a record is a defect in the data
options.misconception: objects to the data, when the fault is in the page's own labelling of it

options.text: The reference numbers, which a reader should be able to understand without a key
options.misconception: objects to the record, when the page is what has failed to explain it

questions.explanation: The title is a line of pipe-separated fragments and it reads the way it is built, which is as a set of fields for a list of results rather than as a sentence for a reader. Results 1-20 of 342 belongs to a listing and tells a reader nothing about what they have found; Household waste collection calendar is the only part that tells them; the trailing Council services is a category in a directory and not part of the title at all. A page title has one job, which is to say what is on the page so that a reader who arrives from a link, a bookmark or a history list knows where they are, and a row of fields defeats that for anyone who did not build the row. The other three answers each find a real weakness in the page, and none of them is the one produced by assembling a title out of index fields.
questions.hint: Ask which part of that line would tell a reader what the page is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A description that repeats the title
questions.learningObjective: judge a page description that adds nothing to a title
questions.stem: A page's description repeats its title with a synonym. What has the page lost?

options.text: A ranking in results, since a description is one of the signals a list uses
options.misconception: invents a ranking effect, when the fault is that the line adds no information at all

options.text: A keyword, since a synonym is still a word the page does not otherwise use
options.misconception: suggests a search effect, which is not what a description is for

options.text: The one place where a reader could have been told what the page settles or contains
Nothing, since repeating a title in other words helps a reader who skimmed
options.misconception: defends the line, when a reader who skimmed the title skims the description too

questions.explanation: A title and a description do two different jobs, and they sit in different places in a reader's path. The title is read on its own, in a list, in a tab, or in a history entry, and it has to identify the page. The description is read where the title is already visible, or where there is room to say more, and it is the only place a page can state what it is for, what it covers, and what a reader will be able to do when they arrive. A synonym spends that place restating the identification. It is worth being clear that this is not a rule about repetition being forbidden: a description that repeats a title is wasting the slot, and a description that adds a date, a scope or a condition is not, because each of those is something the title cannot carry.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could learn from this line that the title has not already told them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Link text that names a destination
questions.learningObjective: judge what a link has to tell a reader before it is followed
questions.stem: A list of results has twenty entries, each a link. Eleven are labelled Read more, four Download form, three are the title of the record, and two are labelled the guidance for this service. Which of these gives a reader the most before the click?

options.text: Read more, since it is the convention and a reader is used to it
options.misconception: leans on convention, when a reader needs to know the destination before leaving the list

options.text: Download form, since it says what kind of thing will arrive
options.misconception: names a type of destination rather than which one, and eleven readers still learn nothing

options.text: The guidance for this service, since it is the longest of the four labels
options.misconception: judges by length, which is the opposite of what makes link text work

options.text: The title of the record, since it names what the reader will be taken to

questions.explanation: A link is a promise about a destination, and the promise is made in the text of the link, because that is all a reader has before they go. Read more names no destination at all, and eleven entries labelled identically are eleven identical promises; a reader scanning a list of forty results learns nothing from any of them and has to open each to find out. Download form does better than Read more because it says something about what kind of thing will arrive, but it is still the same sentence for four different forms, and it tells a reader nothing about which form. The guidance link is the most descriptive and it is the least useful in a list, because it is not a result. The record's own title is the one label that answers the question a reader has before clicking, which is what am I about to be looking at.
questions.hint: Ask which label would still be meaningful in a printed list of the twenty.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: An empty state that apologises
questions.learningObjective: judge what an empty state owes the reader

stimulus.body: EMPTY STATE, shown where a filtered list would appear: Sorry, there is nothing here at the moment. Please check your filters and try again. The list above the state is a filtered list of the reader's own requests, and its filter is set to status: open.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A screen shows, where a filtered list would appear: 'Sorry, there is nothing here at the moment. Please check your filters and try again. The list above the state is a filtered list of the reader's own requests, and its filter is set to status: open.' What has the screen left a reader without?

options.text: Any sense of what the list would contain, so a reader cannot tell whether nothing exists or nothing matched
An apology, since a screen with no results is the screen's fault and not the reader's
options.misconception: treats tone as the problem, when the screen is giving a reader no information at all

options.text: A way to clear the filters, since checking them is not the same as removing them
options.misconception: identifies a real omission and mistakes it for the whole of the failure

options.text: An explanation of why the list is empty, which is the only thing the state is for
options.misconception: states the purpose of the state rather than the fact that the state is not meeting it

questions.explanation: An empty state has to answer a question a reader is now asking, and the question is not why the system is sorry. It is what this list would show, and therefore whether there is nothing to have or whether the reader has asked the wrong question. The screen supplies neither the name of the list nor the number that would have appeared, so a reader cannot distinguish a filter that has excluded everything from a genuinely empty case, and those two need opposite responses. Please check your filters is a reasonable instruction and is not an answer to the question being asked, and it presupposes that filters are in play, which the screen has not established either. The other three answers each name something the state is not doing, and one of them mistakes an instruction for the information a reader needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the list is a list of, and what number it would show.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A loading message that promises a time
questions.learningObjective: judge a wait notice that commits the system to a duration

stimulus.body: WAIT NOTICE: This is taking longer than usual. Expected time: 30 seconds. The notice is shown for the first ten seconds of the wait and does not update. The request is a search over four years of records and the screen shows no progress indicator.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A wait notice reads: 'This is taking longer than usual. Expected time: 30 seconds.' The notice is shown for the first ten seconds of the wait and does not update. The request is a search over four years of records and the screen shows no progress indicator. What is the fault?

options.text: It is shown for only ten seconds, when a slow load needs a notice throughout
options.misconception: objects to the duration of the display, which is not what the sentence commits the system to

options.text: It commits the system to a number it will not correct when the number passes
It says taking longer than usual, so readers are told the system is at fault
options.misconception: reads a diagnosis as an admission, when the notice is meant to explain the wait

options.text: It gives a time rather than an activity, so a reader cannot tell what is happening
options.misconception: misses that a time is exactly the problem and an activity would be the answer

questions.explanation: A wait notice has to be true at the moment it is read and to stay true afterwards, and Expected time: 30 seconds does neither with any confidence. A number stated in a wait notice is a promise, and this one is fixed at the start of a wait whose length the system does not yet know, and it is not updated as the wait goes on, so at some point in every slow load the notice is lying by omission. A reader who has been told to expect thirty seconds and is still waiting at thirty-one has learned something quite different from a reader who was told the wait is taking longer than usual and no worse than that. This is taking longer than usual is honest and vague, and vagueness is exactly right when the alternative is a false precision.
questions.hint: Ask what the notice says at the moment the thirty seconds are up.

questions.topic: A missing-page notice that blames the reader
questions.learningObjective: judge a not-found notice written from the wrong side

stimulus.body: PAGE NOT FOUND: 404. The page you are looking for does not exist. Please check the address you typed and try again. There is no link to the site's home page or to any section index.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A page reads: 'PAGE NOT FOUND: 404. The page you are looking for does not exist. Please check the address you typed and try again. There is no link to the site's home page or to any section index.' What has the notice got wrong?

options.text: It says the page does not exist, when a server error may be the real cause

options.text: It gives a status number, which a reader has no use for and cannot act on

options.text: It assumes the reader typed the address, when most of them followed a link they did not write

options.misconception: misdescribes a real omission as something a notice must never do

questions.explanation: Please check the address you typed makes a claim about how the reader arrived, and most of them did not type anything. They followed a link from a search result, a message, a page whose link has been moved, or a bookmark from years ago, and a notice that begins by faulting their typing is addressing a small minority of the people who will see it. The remedy costs one clause, and it is the clause that makes the difference between a notice and an excuse: the address may be wrong, or the link may be old, and the reader needs to be able to act on either. That no link back to the home page appears is a genuine and serious omission, and it is not a rule that a notice should never contain navigation, since a notice with no way forward is a dead end by design.
questions.hint: Ask how most of the readers who see this notice got here.

questions.stem: A first screen is headed 'Welcome' and reads: 'Import your existing records now to get started. A file in CSV format, up to 20MB, may be dropped anywhere on this screen. Records may also be added one at a time later.' What has the screen not done for a reader meeting it first?

options.text: Explained what CSV is, since most readers meeting this first will not know
options.misconception: asks for a glossary, which the screen does supply in the phrase a file in CSV format

options.text: Said how long the import takes, which every first screen should estimate
options.misconception: demands an estimate the screen has no basis to give

options.text: Said what a record is here, so a first-time reader does not have to guess what is being asked for

questions.hint: Ask what the reader is being asked to bring, and where the screen tells them what that is.

questions.stem: A notice reads: 'You are using the free plan. Upgrade now to unlock unlimited projects, priority support and team sharing.' The notice gives no price and no billing period, and the buttons read Upgrade and See what's included. What has the notice withheld?

options.text: What the upgrade costs and for how long, so a reader cannot judge the offer being pressed on them

options.text: How to cancel, which a notice is not the right place for

options.text: Whether the free plan will be lost on upgrading, which a reader may reasonably fear
options.misconception: raises a real fear, but the price is what the notice is obliged to supply

questions.explanation: A notice that presses a reader towards a button owes that reader the figure that makes the button mean something. Upgrade is not an offer until a reader knows what it costs, for what period, and on what terms, and a notice that names three features and omits all three of those is not being brief: it is being selective in the one direction that helps the seller. The notice is not a contract and need not print terms, but the price and the period are the two facts a reader cannot supply from anywhere else, and they are the two a reader on a free plan is most likely to want before pressing anything. The three features are named, so that part is done; cancelling belongs somewhere a reader can find after they have agreed rather than in a notice that is trying to get a click.

questions.stem: A notice reads: 'Ready to stop losing money on your current plan? Upgrade today and keep every one of your projects while you do it. Cancel any time.' The buttons read 'Yes, upgrade now' and 'No thanks'. What has the notice done?

options.text: Offerred a way out, since Cancel any time is printed in the body of the notice
options.misconception: credits the notice with an exit and misses the loaded question that precedes it

options.text: Taken the answer into the question, so a reader who disagrees has to say no to a loaded phrase
Asked a question rather than a statement, which is the wrong form for a notice
options.misconception: objects to a form, when the defect is in what the question assumes

options.text: Used a second person, which an offer notice should avoid
options.misconception: objects to a pronoun, when every other objection here is about the question itself

questions.explanation: Ready to stop losing money is not a question, it is a claim wearing the punctuation of one, and the claim is the problem. Money is being lost on a free plan: not having unlimited projects is not a loss, and a reader who knows that has to reject the whole premise before the question can be answered, which is a much harder thing to do than answering a question. The second button then completes the trap, because No thanks is an acceptance of a framing rather than a refusal of an offer, and a reader who is indifferent is nudged toward the button that ends the notice. Cancel any time in the body is a real disclosure and does not repair any of this, since a reader has to reach the body to find it and the question has already been asked.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who believes they are losing nothing has to do with that question.

questions.stem: A request reads: 'To send you reminders about your appointments, this app needs access to your calendar. Allow access so you never miss an appointment.' The buttons read 'Allow access' and 'Not now'. What has the request done?

options.text: Named what is being collected, which the request does in its first line
options.misconception: credits the request with a disclosure and misses what it has done with the asking

options.text: Explained why access is needed, which most requests never do at all
options.misconception: credits a justification the request supplies and mistakes it for the fault

options.text: Argued for the answer before asking the question, so the second button is the harder press
Offerred a later choice, since Not now is different from a refusal
options.misconception: reads a deferral as an exit, when the request is what has made the deferral costly

questions.explanation: The first line states a purpose and the second line argues for the conclusion, and the button labels then make the two answers uneven. So you never miss an appointment is not an instruction and not a condition, it is a benefit placed in the imperative so that it reads as the reason the question has only one comfortable answer. A reader who does not want an app reading a calendar has to press the button that sounds like a postponement of something they have already declined, and a reader who closes the dialog has refused nothing because the dialog was never framed as a decision. Naming what is collected and giving a reason are both things a good request does, and this one does them, which is what makes the framing easy to miss.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who does not want calendar access has to press.

questions.learningObjective: judge a notification that gives news and no way to act on it

stimulus.body: NOTIFICATION: 2 documents need your signature. The notification shows the names of the two documents, their sizes and the date each was sent, and no button. Tapping the notification opens the document list rather than the document.

questions.stem: A notification reads: '2 documents need your signature.' It shows the names of the two documents, their sizes and the date each was sent, and no button. Tapping the notification opens the document list rather than the document. What has the notification failed to do?

options.text: Name the documents, since the notification does list both by name
options.misconception: misses the names the notification already supplies and names the missing action instead

options.text: Say how urgent the signing is, which a reader cannot judge from a date
options.misconception: raises a real omission that is secondary to the missing route to the action

options.text: Give the names of the senders, since a signature should know who wants it
options.misconception: asks for a disclosure, where the fault is that the named documents cannot be reached from the notice

options.text: Offer a route to the action, so a reader who is notified has to go and look for the thing

questions.explanation: A notification is a message that arrives when a reader is not looking at the thing it is about, so its first duty is to carry the reader back to the action. This one names the two documents, which is genuinely useful information, and then sends the reader to the list rather than to either document, so a reader who taps has to find the file again before they can sign it. Every field the notification shows, the size, the date sent, is a fact about the past, and none of them is a step. Note the interaction with need: a notice that says something needs your signature is making a claim about the reader's obligations, and it is a poor form to use one if the reader then has to reconstruct where the obligation is.
questions.hint: Ask where a reader ends up after tapping, and what they have to find.

stimulus.body: BANNER: We have updated the way we handle account numbers. Existing account numbers have not changed. No date appears on the banner and no date appears anywhere in the text.

questions.stem: A banner reads: 'We have updated the way we handle account numbers. Existing account numbers have not changed.' No date appears on the banner or in the text. What has the notice left a reader without?

options.text: A date, since a reader cannot tell whether this has already happened to their account
The reassurance, which the second sentence supplies in plain words
options.misconception: credits the notice with a reassurance and misses the element it is actually missing

options.text: A person to write to, which every notice about an account should name
options.misconception: raises a real omission, and the date is what the notice is actually missing

options.text: A second paragraph, since one line of text is too little for a change of this kind
options.misconception: judges by length, when the fault is a missing date rather than a missing paragraph

questions.explanation: A notice about a change exists so that a reader can work out whether it applies to them, and the question it always raises first is when. We have updated is a completed act with no date on it, and a reader with an account has no way to tell whether the change happened last week, happens tonight, or is scheduled for a date they have not been given. The second sentence narrows the alarm without answering it, because the numbers have not changed and something else has, and the something else is precisely what a dated notice would have specified. questions.hint: Ask whether a reader can tell when the change happened to them.

questions.stem: A banner reads: 'To keep the site working we use cookies. You can accept all cookies for a faster experience.' The buttons read 'Accept all' and 'Manage settings'. The banner is shown once, on a reader's first visit, and carries no link to any description of what cookies are. What has the banner done?

options.text: Offered a second option, which is what a notice about cookies has to do
options.misconception: credits the notice with a choice and misses the comparison it has already decided

options.text: Told the reader that accepting is faster, so the comparison between the buttons is settled in advance
Defined cookies, which a reader who has never met the word will not know
options.misconception: fixes on an absent definition rather than on what the notice says about its first option

options.text: Placed itself at the top of the page, so that no reader can miss it
options.misconception: credits a placement and passes the bias between the two buttons entirely

questions.explanation: The banner does offer a choice, and the presence of a second button is not by itself a problem. A reader choosing between Accept all and Manage settings is therefore not comparing what the two do, since one of them is described as faster and the other is not described at all, and a reader with a preference for managing settings is being argued out of it rather than being given the facts. The defect is easy to miss precisely because the notice looks scrupulous: it has a settings option, and it has not noticed that the sentence before the buttons has already settled the vote.
questions.hint: Ask what the second sentence tells the reader about the button it does not name.

questions.stem: An image is described in the file as: 'A bar chart. The horizontal axis is labelled Year, running 2014 to 2025. The vertical axis is labelled Users in thousands, from 0 to 400, with a gridline every 50. The bars rise from 120 in 2014 to 355 in 2025, rising in every year.' The caption reads 'Chart of users, 2014 to 2025' and the alternative text reads 'Chart of users, 2014 to 2025'. What has the alternative text done?

options.misconception: credits the alternative with economy, and its problem is that it duplicates

options.text: Left out the rising trend, which is the one thing the caption should have carried
options.misconception: invents a claim about the caption, and the failure is the duplication of it

options.text: Repeated the caption, so a reader using it gets no axis, no scale and no value

options.misconception: fixes on a word that is accurate while the duplication goes unremarked

options.text: Left the caption to do the work, which is the correct division of labour
options.misconception: invents a caption, since the file records that none is printed

options.misconception: supplies an exemption the presence of the text already contradicts

options.text: The counts should be rounded, since a list of twelve is not a useful figure to show

options.text: A relative date is shorter to write, so the copy is efficient as it stands

options.text: The article is longer, so it will rank lower in a list of results

options.text: Capitalised only one item, so the row is not consistent in its case

options.misconception: raises a real consistency problem and misses the one inside the row

options.text: A reason to use capitals at all, which a list of options does not need
options.misconception: objects to capitals, when the case is doing a job the page has not explained

options.text: A shorter set of four, since a reader should not have to choose between two kinds of record

questions.stem: Headings run down a settings page as follows: 'Notifications | Choose what gets sent | Email and text | Turn things off'. Under the third there are two controls, both off. What has the page done?

options.text: Used the imperative in the last heading, so it should sit beside the controls it names
options.misconception: fixes on one heading and misses the mixture of forms across all four

options.text: Used a heading too short to be useful, so Notifications should name the section more fully
options.misconception: judges by length, when the fault is the mixture of grammatical forms

options.text: Mixed capitalisation, so a reader cannot scan the four headings as a set
options.misconception: objects to case, when the three forms are the thing that stops a reader scanning

options.text: Mixed a noun, an instruction and an imperative, so a reader cannot tell which are names and which are actions

questions.hint: Ask which of these four are names and which are actions, and where the page says.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The parts of a help article
questions.learningObjective: order the elements of a task-based help article
questions.stem: A reader has arrived at a help article with a task they cannot complete. Put the five parts in the order the article needs them.

options.text: What the reader is trying to do, so the article is about their task and not about the system
What will happen if they do it, so they can judge before they act
The steps, in the order in which they have to be carried out
What to do when a step does not work, so the failure is already handled
Where to go for help if none of this has worked for them

questions.explanation: The article has to start where the reader is, which is a task, not a product. A reader who has arrived with something they cannot do is not looking for a description of the feature and will close a page that opens with one, so the first move is to name the task in the reader's terms. The second is the consequence, and it comes before the steps because a step is a commitment and a reader who does not know what the steps will do cannot judge whether to make it. The steps follow, in order, with the branch points in them, because that is the material the reader came for. The failure section comes next and not earlier, since a reader who has not yet tried the steps does not need it, and it is the section that most often shows up before the steps by accident. The last move is the one a reader reaches only when the rest has failed, and putting it first is a common way of avoiding a support queue rather than reducing it.
questions.hint: Ask where the reader is when they arrive, and what they have to decide before they act.

questions.stem: A notice reads: 'Your session will expire in 10 minutes due to inactivity. Save your work now or it will be lost. Any unsaved changes cannot be recovered.' The form has been open four minutes and the reader is typing in the last field. What is the fault?

options.text: It gives a countdown with no date, so a reader cannot tell when the ten minutes began
options.misconception: misses that the notice names both a duration and a cause

options.text: It says the session expires, when what expires is the reader's patience
options.misconception: objects to a technical term, where the fault is the certainty of the consequence

options.text: It states a settled loss where there is only a possible one, so a reader may give up work to avoid it
It warns a reader who may not yet be able to save, since the last field is not finished
options.misconception: invents a second defect, when the loss is the part being announced as settled

questions.explanation: Two of the three sentences announce as finished something that has not happened. Your session will expire in 10 minutes is a statement about the future and is true. Save your work now or it will be lost makes the loss the outcome of doing nothing, and Any unsaved changes cannot be recovered removes the possibility of getting the work back even if the reader does save it, which is a different and much stronger claim than the first. Both are stated in the present tense, which in interface copy is the tense of fact, so a reader is being told that a loss has occurred. The reader described in the file is four minutes in and typing, so the notice is aimed at exactly the person for whom the certainty does most harm: someone who will stop what they are doing to go and find out what is already gone.
questions.hint: Ask which of these sentences would still be true if the reader saved immediately.

questions.topic: A notice with an action and no clock
questions.learningObjective: judge what a notification must say about how long an offer lasts
questions.stem: A notification reads 'Your export is ready to download' and offers a Download button. The file is kept for seven days. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing, since the button is there and a reader can act on the notice at once
options.misconception: credits an action and passes the limit that follows from dismissing the notice

options.text: A sentence saying the export succeeded, since ready to download already implies it
options.misconception: asks for a restatement, and the retention period is the real omission

options.text: The file's size, which a reader needs before deciding whether to download it
options.misconception: demands a detail when the seven days are what the notice must state

options.text: The seven days, so a reader who dismisses the notice has no way to know when it goes

questions.explanation: A notification is a message a reader will probably dismiss, and the design has to assume they will. Dismissed, a notification has left the reader with a fact and a button they have not pressed, and if the fact is that a file exists and nothing about how long it will exist, then a reader who comes back in a fortnight finds a broken button and has no way of knowing whether the export failed or the file was cleaned up. The seven days is the fact that makes the button worth pressing and the fact a reader needs in order to decide whether to press it now or later. This is the same requirement as a deadline in any short piece of writing: a resource that expires has to say so at the point where the reader is deciding.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader knows on Thursday about a file they have not downloaded.

questions.topic: A heading that marks nothing
questions.learningObjective: judge a heading that does not delimit its group
questions.stem: A settings page carries the single heading Account above three controls, with nothing after them on the page. What has the heading failed to do?

options.text: Mark where its group stops, so a reader cannot tell whether anything follows it
Name the page, which is already shown in the browser's title bar
options.misconception: credits a name given elsewhere, and the heading on the page is a boundary

options.text: Give the three controls a shared description, which a single word cannot supply
options.misconception: asks more of a heading than a heading is for

options.text: Say which of the three settings it covers, so a reader does not have to guess
options.misconception: demands a contents list, and the missing thing is where the group ends

questions.explanation: A heading on a settings page does two things, and the second is the one that goes missing here. It names the group, which Account does, and it closes the group, which tells a reader that the controls beneath it are the whole of that group and that anything further down the page belongs to something else. A one-word heading with three controls under it and nothing after them gives a reader no way to tell whether there is a fourth control that has not loaded, or a second group that has lost its own heading, or whether the page simply ends. The cost is highest on the page where a reader is about to change something, because the reader who cannot tell where the group ends cannot tell what else the change will affect. Naming the page, describing the controls and listing them are all things a heading is not for.
questions.hint: Ask a reader where the group headed Account stops.

questions.topic: A screen whose subject is the system
questions.learningObjective: judge copy that describes the product rather than the reader's task

stimulus.body: WELCOME SCREEN. Heading: We think you will love this. Body: We have designed this to make your life easier, and we are sure you will find it useful. The screen has no image, no example, and no statement of what the product does.

questions.stem: A welcome screen is headed 'We think you will love this' and its body reads: 'We have designed this to make your life easier, and we are sure you will find it useful.' The screen has no image, no example and no statement of what the product does. What has the screen failed to do?

options.text: Be welcoming, which a welcome screen is supposed to be
options.misconception: answers a different question, and every one of these sentences is welcoming

options.text: Say what the reader can do, since every sentence has the product as its subject
Use the word you more than the word we, which is the ordinary advice for copy
options.misconception: counts pronouns, and the fault is the choice of subject rather than its number

options.text: Include an image, since a welcome screen with a picture works better than one without
options.misconception: demands a visual element, when the fault is that the text is about the wrong thing

questions.explanation: Read the two sentences and ask what a reader has learned. We have designed this, we are sure you will find it useful, and you will love this are three statements about the people who made the thing and about what they think of it. None of them is about what the thing does, and so a reader who has arrived to do something has learned nothing that would let them decide whether to go on. This is the characteristic failure of a welcome screen written by the team that built the product, because the team knows what the product does and the reader does not, and a first screen is the one place where that difference can be closed for free. questions.learningObjective: judge a summary a reader cannot place themselves in

stimulus.body: SUMMARY at the top of a help article headed Setting up single sign-on: This guide covers SSO configuration for tenants using SAML 2.0. It assumes you have already provisioned the IdP and that you hold the tenant admin role. Most teams finish in under an hour.

questions.stem: A summary reads: 'This guide covers SSO configuration for tenants using SAML 2.0. It assumes you have already provisioned the IdP and that you hold the tenant admin role. Most teams finish in under an hour.' What has the summary left a reader without?

options.text: How long the article takes, which the summary gives as under an hour
options.misconception: misses the estimate the summary does in fact supply

options.text: Which steps are optional, since a summary that assumes prior work cannot list them
options.misconception: raises a real omission, and the undefined terms come before the question of optional steps

options.text: What the four terms are, so a reader cannot tell whether this article is about their situation
A link to the article's own contents list, which every long article needs
options.misconception: demands a contents list, and the reader's first obstacle is the vocabulary

questions.explanation: A summary has to place a reader in the article, and this one cannot do that for the readers who most need it. It assumes you have already provisioned is the sentence that makes the article unusable for somebody, and it is aimed at exactly the readers who were going to abandon the page, which is the wrong way round. A summary has room to name what the article is for in words a reader who has not met the field can use, and the field's own terms belong below it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must already know before the summary tells them anything useful.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A term that changes under the reader
questions.learningObjective: compare two sections and find where the term has moved

stimulus.body: Section one, headed What we mean by a project: A project is a container for documents. Everyone in the tenant can see every project unless the project is set to private. Section two, headed Deleting a project: Deleting a project deletes everything in it for everyone, including people who never opened it. If a project is private, deleting it still removes it from the tenant's list of projects for its owner.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: Two sections of a help article read: 'Section one, headed What we mean by a project: A project is a container for documents. Everyone in the tenant can see every project unless the project is set to private.' and 'Section two, headed Deleting a project: Deleting a project deletes everything in it for everyone, including people who never opened it. If a project is private, deleting it still removes it from the tenant's list of projects for its owner.' What has happened to the word project between the two sections?

options.text: Been given two meanings deliberately, so a reader has to read both sections to be sure
options.misconception: reads a deliberate ambiguity, where the second section simply contradicts the first

options.text: Been used both for the container and for the list it appears in, which is a common slip
options.misconception: invents a second sense, and the disagreement between the sections is about visibility

options.text: Stayed the same, since both sections describe one object in different words
options.misconception: denies the change, and the first section's exception is the thing the second removes

options.text: It has been given an exception in the first and overridden by the second, and nothing says so

questions.explanation: The two sections disagree and neither notices. Section one says everyone in the tenant can see every project unless the project is set to private, so private is the exception. Section two says deleting a project deletes everything in it for everyone, including people who never opened it, which is the rule, and then adds that if a project is private, deleting it still removes it from the list for its owner, which is a third thing and is not the same as the second thing. A reader who read section one and is now deleting something cannot tell whether a private project is being deleted for everyone or only struck from its owner's list. Nothing in section two refers back to section one, so the reader has no signal that anything has changed. This is the ordinary way a term drifts in a long document: not by being redefined, which would be announced, but by an exception being added in one place and quietly removed in another.
questions.hint: Ask what a private project is in each section, and whether the second refers back to the first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A record that is deleted and a record that is permanent
questions.learningObjective: weigh a closing claim against what the article has already said

stimulus.body: ARTICLE, section What a report is. It opens: A report is a question you ask of the data, and running it gives you an answer. Halfway down, the section says that reports are stored for 90 days, after which the answer is deleted. It closes: A report is a permanent record of what the data showed on the day you asked.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A section reads: 'A report is a question you ask of the data, and running it gives you an answer.' Halfway down it says reports are stored for 90 days, after which the answer is deleted. It closes: 'A report is a permanent record of what the data showed on the day you asked.' What is the strongest objection to the last sentence?

options.text: The section says the answer is deleted after 90 days, so nothing it produces is permanent
The word permanent is too strong for anything about data, which is always changing
options.misconception: objects to the word in general when the section has supplied a specific 90-day rule

options.text: The first sentence makes a report a question, and a question cannot be a record
options.misconception: takes the opening and the ending as irreconcilable, when the deletion rule is the contradiction

options.text: The section gives no date, so a reader cannot tell when the 90 days began
options.misconception: asks about a missing date, which is a separate and much smaller gap

questions.explanation: The closing sentence is contradicted by a rule the same section has already laid down, and the contradiction is about a word with a number attached to it. Reports are stored for 90 days, after which the answer is deleted, is not a matter of emphasis or of the general mutability of data; it is a retention period, and a permanent record is by definition one that is not deleted. A reader deciding whether to rely on a report as evidence is the reader the sentence is for, and they are the reader most damaged by it, because the sentence tells them to keep something the section says will be removed. It is worth noticing the shape of the writing: the opening and the closing are both in the register of a definition, and the rule in the middle is in the register of a fact, and the section never reconciles the two.
questions.hint: Ask what the middle of the section says happens after 90 days.

questions.topic: An article that assumes the cause
questions.learningObjective: judge a help article that opens on one of several possible causes

stimulus.body: HELP ARTICLE, headed Exports and permissions. It opens: Exports run with the permissions of the person who schedules them, not the person who downloads them. It then sets out team roles, how folder permissions are inherited, and a table of role names. The article carries no statement of what a reader should try first.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A help article headed 'Exports and permissions' opens: 'Exports run with the permissions of the person who schedules them, not the person who downloads them.' It then covers team roles, inherited folder permissions and a table of role names, and never says what a reader should try first. What has the article failed to do?

options.text: Give the permissions attached to each role, which the table is there to supply
options.misconception: asks for a detail the article does provide, in its own table

options.text: Ask what the reader's problem is, so a reader whose problem is not permissions has a way out
Say how long an export takes, since a reader planning one will want to know
options.misconception: demands a duration, and the fault is the unexamined cause

options.text: Offer a way to change a role, which a reader who needs one will be looking for
options.misconception: asks for a remedy in an article about diagnosis rather than about granting

questions.explanation: The article is well made inside its own scope and that is the difficulty. It explains a real mechanism, the permissions of the scheduler rather than of the downloader, which is genuinely the sort of thing a reader cannot work out, and then it supplies the reference material a reader would need to check the mechanism against their own situation. What it never does is ask, or establish, that permissions are the reader's problem. Exports fail for at least four ordinary reasons and an article that opens on one of them gives a reader with any of the other three a page that is confident, detailed and useless to them. The omission of a first step compounds it, because the reader has no way to find out whether they are in the article's case before they have read the table.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader whose export fails for another reason should do with this page.

questions.topic: A control that names no object
questions.learningObjective: judge a control whose action cannot be guessed

stimulus.body: BUTTON ROW: Save changes | Cancel | Discard. The page carries no other text near the row, and the third control is on its own at the right-hand end of the row. The row sits at the foot of a settings page, below twelve controls, with no heading near it.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A button row reads: 'Save changes | Cancel | Discard'. There is no other text near the row and the third control sits on its own at the right-hand end. The row sits at the foot of a settings page, below twelve controls, with no heading near it. What has the row done?

options.text: Put Cancel beside Save changes, though the two are not opposites and a reader may expect them to be
options.misconception: objects to a conventional pairing, and the fault is the third control's missing object

options.text: Ordered the row wrongly, since Discard belongs at the left where nothing else competes with it
options.misconception: proposes a layout change when the fault is in what the third control says

options.text: Left one control with no object, so a reader cannot tell what it discards or what it keeps
Mixed a three-word label with a one-word one, when they should be the same length
options.misconception: judges by length, and the fault is a control with no object at all

questions.explanation: Save changes and Cancel each name an object, the changes and nothing, and both can be understood without any further text. Discard cannot, because a discard is always of something and this row does not say what. The word is also ambiguous in a second way, because a discard in an editing interface can mean the last change or the whole document, and a reader about to press a control whose label is a single bare verb at the end of a row of two safe labels has to guess. This is why destructive controls are given the object even when the object is in a heading, and why the position at the end of the row, separated from the others, makes the ambiguity worse rather than better: separation signals that this one is different, without saying in what.
questions.hint: Ask what the third control acts on, and how a reader would find out.

options.misconception: objects to a field in a system when the reader's problem is the missing condition

options.text: A list of streets with no times, so a reader cannot tell when the charges apply
options.misconception: raises a real omission, and the date has no second home anywhere on the page

options.text: A condition stated once, so a reader part of the way down has lost the date the figures depend on

questions.topic: Results a reader cannot reach
questions.learningObjective: compute how much of a result set the pagination exposes
questions.stem: A search page carries the header 'Results 1 to 10 of 247' and a page control reading 'Page 1 of 24', with a page size of 10 and no other size offered. How much of the result set can a reader reach by paging?

options.text: Two hundred and forty of the two hundred and forty-seven, so seven results are unreachable
All of them, because the header names two hundred and forty-seven and the count is authoritative
options.misconception: takes the header at face value, when the page control is what limits what can be shown

options.text: Two hundred and fifty, because twenty-four full pages of ten hold the whole set
options.misconception: multiplies the pages by the size without noticing that 24 x 10 is less than 247

options.text: Nothing at all, since a page control that disagrees with the header has broken the page
options.misconception: supposes a total failure, when the first twenty-four pages work perfectly well

What makes this worth an item is that nothing on the page looks broken. A reader reaches page 24, the list is full, and there is no page 25, and a reader who wants the last seven results has no route to them and no indication that they exist. The header, which is the only place the true count appears, is the one element that does not govern what is reachable.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of pages by the page size and compare with the count in the header.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A share printed above the table that produced it
questions.learningObjective: check a summary figure against the figures it summarises
questions.stem: A page prints the line 'Top 5 account types make up 94% of all queries' above a table of the top five, with counts 41,200, 12,900, 3,050, 1,140 and 610. The page states the total number of queries recorded as 64,000. What can a reader establish?

options.text: That the top five are the wrong five, since a sixth type would have to be larger than the fifth
options.misconception: proposes a different set, and the fault is the share printed above the set that is given

options.text: That the five counts give about ninety-two per cent, so the line and the table disagree
That the total is too low, since the five counts add to more than the total
options.misconception: asserts the opposite; the five counts come to 58,900 against a stated 64,000

options.text: That queries were counted twice, so no share printed on the page can be trusted
options.misconception: supplies a mechanism the page gives no evidence for

questions.explanation: Add the five counts and they come to 58,900, and 58,900 out of 64,000 is 92.03 per cent, which rounds to 92 and not to 94. The check can be done two ways: sum the counts and divide, or note that the remaining 5,100 is 7.97 per cent and that the two shares must add to exactly one, which they do, which confirms the arithmetic and confirms that 94 was not what the table yields. The gap is two percentage points, which is not a rounding artefact, and it is not a rounding artefact in the direction of generosity to the page's own headline either. A reader can go further than noticing a mismatch: the true share is below the printed one, so the page has understated the share of the rest, and whichever figure is right, the two lines on the page cannot both be.
questions.hint: Add the five counts, divide by the total, and compare the result with the printed figure.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What a destructive warning must carry
questions.learningObjective: select the elements of a warning that lets a reader refuse
questions.stem: A control removes data and cannot be undone. Which three things must the warning that appears before it carry?

options.text: What will be removed and how much of it, so the reader can size the loss
That the action cannot be undone, so the decision is final rather than reversible
What the reader can do instead, if there is any route that keeps the data
The name of whoever can undo the action afterwards, if there is such a person
options.misconception: assumes undo is possible, when the whole point of the warning is that it is not

options.text: How many support cases this action has generated, so a reader can weigh the risk
options.misconception: asks for an internal figure that a reader has no use for

options.text: A complete itemised list of everything affected, however long that list turns out to be
options.misconception: demands completeness, which is what a count and a description are for

questions.explanation: A warning before an irreversible action has to support a decision, and a decision needs three things. What is going, and how much, because a reader who is looking at a list of six documents and a list of six hundred needs to know which warning they are reading. That it is final, because cannot be undone is the whole difference between a warning and a confirmation and it is the phrase a reader will quote back to themselves afterwards. And what the alternative is, if there is one, because a warning with no alternative leaves a reader to choose between doing nothing and losing something, which is a worse pair of options than any a system should offer. The three that do not matter each add a burden without adding a decision: a person who can undo it contradicts the premise, a support statistic is noise, and an itemised list is impossible for any real removal.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs in order to decide against the action, not merely to recognise it.

questions.topic: Why copy written last goes wrong
questions.learningObjective: reason about the consequences of the order in which copy is written
questions.stem: Interface text is usually written after the feature it describes has been finished and shipped. What is the strongest consequence of that order of work?

options.text: The text is shorter, which is an advantage on a small screen and costs nothing
options.misconception: praises a side effect, and the question asks about the cost

options.text: The words are checked by the people who built the feature, so they are more accurate than a reader's
options.misconception: assumes accuracy follows from access to the system, which is not what the order damages

options.text: The writer meets a finished system and describes it, rather than meeting a reader with a problem
The text is written by people who know the system best, so it is closer to the truth than a user's would be
options.misconception: assumes expertise produces usable copy, and that assumption is the problem

questions.explanation: The order decides what the writer is looking at. Write the words first and you are looking at a problem, a reader who cannot do a thing and a description of what would help, and the words that come out of that describe the reader's situation. Write them last and you are looking at an implementation, which is fully working and fully explained by its own design, and the words that come out of that describe the implementation. This is why shipped copy so often uses the system's internal vocabulary, why error messages name states rather than actions, and why help articles are organised around the feature tree rather than around tasks: all three are symptoms of writing to the artefact instead of to the reader. The other three answers each credit the order with something, and each of those somethings is a benefit of a process whose cost falls on the people using it.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer is looking at when the words are written.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Rewriting a destructive warning
questions.learningObjective: say what a warning owes a reader and rewrite it
questions.stem: A confirmation reads: 'Are you sure? This cannot be undone.' It appears when a reader presses Delete on a project, the project contains 14 documents, and three people besides the reader have access. In three or four sentences, say what the notice has to do to be worth showing, and rewrite it.

answer.exemplar: The notice has to let a reader tell what is about to be lost, how much of it there is, and who else is affected, and it has to put those things where the reader is actually looking, which is the two buttons. As printed it has none of them: are you sure is addressed to nobody, this cannot be undone is the one true and useful sentence, and three people having access is a fact the notice silently ignores. A version that works is: 'Delete this project and its 14 documents? The three people with access will lose access to it. This cannot be undone.' The word that matters most in the rewrite is 14, because a reader who is looking at a long list of documents has no way to size the loss without a count, and the clause about the other three people is what turns a warning about the reader's own screen into a warning about other people. A good answer will keep the count and the access clause and will put them before the buttons rather than after.

questions.explanation: A confirmation is judged by one question, which is whether a reader can tell, without leaving the notice, what they are agreeing to and what it costs. This one cannot, and the reason is not tone or length: it is that the notice contains no noun that a reader can picture, no number they can size, and no mention of anyone else. The two things a good rewrite must recover are the object with its count and the people affected, and a third that costs nothing and is often left out, which is that the action is being taken in a shared space rather than a private one. The test for a good answer is whether the rewritten buttons can be read in isolation from the page: if a reader who has lost their place can still tell what they are about to press, the notice has done its work.
questions.hint: Ask what noun is missing from the sentence a reader is being asked to agree to.
