questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Rewriting a notification that reports nothing
questions.learningObjective: say what a notification must carry and rewrite it
questions.stem: A notification reads '1 comment'. Tapping it opens a list of six comments, of which one is unread and that one is not the newest. In three or four sentences, say what this notification has failed to carry, and rewrite it.

answer.exemplar: The notification has failed to say three things: who is waiting, which comment is the unread one, and what a reader gets by opening it. One comment is a count of the wrong thing, because a reader's question on seeing a comment notification is who is waiting for a reply, and the notification gives a number where it should have given a name. Tapping opens a list of six rather than the comment itself, so the reader has to find the unread one, and the fact that the unread one is not the newest means the reader has to read to find it. A version that works: 'Ruth Ilori commented on 'March timetable' 2 hours ago. Open the comment.' The name, the thing, the time and the destination have replaced the number, and the count has not been lost so much as demoted to the one case where it is the most useful thing to say, which is when there is more than one.

questions.explanation: A notification has a very small job and almost no room, and the job is to make a reader decide to open it. One comment does none of the things that job requires. It does not say who is waiting, so a reader cannot judge whether the comment matters to them. It does not say what it is on, so a reader who has six of these cannot tell which one this is. And because the destination is the list rather than the comment, and the unread one is not the newest, the notification sends the reader to do the finding that the notification existed to do. The discipline in rewriting this is to resist adding words and to work out which single fact would have made the difference, because a notification that carries one usable fact beats one that carries three approximate ones.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs to know before deciding to open the notification.

The export uses the same permissions model as the report screen, so if you cannot see the data in Reports the export will be empty. The note appears in a single column and has no subheadings.

questions.stem: A release note reads: 'As a system administrator you can now export audit logs, and end users will find the same data under Reports. The export uses the same permissions model as the report screen, so if you cannot see the data in Reports the export will be empty.' It has no subheadings. What has the note done?

options.text: Named the role of administrator, when a release note should address only the person reading it
options.misconception: objects to naming two roles, when the fault is what one sentence asks both of them to do

options.text: Assumed the reader can see the data in Reports, which not every reader can
options.misconception: fixes on an assumption the note in fact states and handles

options.text: Made permissions a subject of a release note, when that belongs in a help article
options.misconception: objects to the content when the fault is the single address

options.text: Written one line for two readers, so each has to find their own case and what follows from it

questions.explanation: A release note is read by two populations and they need different sentences from it, and the usual way to serve both is to serve neither. The first sentence opens with a role, gives that reader their fact, and then appends a second fact addressed to a different role in the same grammatical frame, so a system administrator has to read past the end-users clause and an end user has to read past the first one. The second sentence is worse, because the consequence it describes, an empty export, is the administrator's problem while the test it gives, whether you can see the data in Reports, is the end user's. The note is not wrong and it is not long; it is single-addressed by construction, and the subheadings it lacks are the cheapest available repair.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two readers each of the two sentences is for.

questions.topic: An error that names a cause it cannot know
questions.learningObjective: judge a message that attributes a cause it has no evidence for

stimulus.body: ERROR MESSAGE: Your session expired because you were idle. You were inactive for 34 minutes. The system's own log for the same period records requests from the same session at 6 minutes and at 19 minutes, and the message does not say where the figure of 34 came from.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A message reads: 'Your session expired because you were idle. You were inactive for 34 minutes.' The system's log for the same period records requests from that session at 6 and at 19 minutes, and the message does not say where 34 came from. What has the message claimed?

options.text: That a cause and a duration were measured, when the log shows activity inside the period
That the session expired, which the message states and which nothing disputes
options.misconception: credits a correct statement and misses the claim built on top of it

options.text: That 34 minutes is too long a period, so the timeout itself is set wrongly
options.misconception: proposes a different setting, when the message has claimed a cause it cannot know

options.text: That the reader was reading rather than away, since reading sends no requests
options.misconception: infers behaviour the log cannot show, which is exactly the message's own fault

questions.explanation: The message makes two claims and the second is the one that fails. Your session expired is true and is the fact the reader needs. Because you were idle is a cause, and it is a claim about what the reader was doing, and it is contradicted by the log the message itself sits on top of: requests at 6 and 19 minutes mean the session was being used inside the 34-minute period the message calls inactivity. The message cannot repair this by being more certain, because the certainty is the fault; it can only stop asserting a cause. A reader who believes the message will conclude that they were away, that the timeout is generous, and that nothing needs investigating, and all three are wrong. A message that said only that the session ended after 34 minutes without a request would be shorter, correct, and would still be worth showing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the log supports the word idle.
